**Judges 1**
*Now after the death of Joshua it came to pass, that the children of Israel asked the Lord, saying, Who shall go up for us against the Canaanites first, to fight against them?*

*2 And the Lord said, Judah shall go up: behold, I have delivered the land into his hand.*

*3 And Judah said unto Simeon his brother, Come up with me into my lot, that we may fight against the Canaanites; and I likewise will go with thee into thy lot. So Simeon went with him.*

*4 And Judah went up; and the Lord delivered the Canaanites and the Perizzites into their hand: and they slew of them in Bezek ten thousand men.*

*5 And they found Adonibezek in Bezek: and they fought against him, and they slew the Canaanites and the Perizzites.*

*6 But Adonibezek fled; and they pursued after him, and caught him, and cut off his thumbs and his great toes.*

*7 And Adonibezek said, Threescore and ten kings, having their thumbs and their great toes cut off, gathered their meat under my table: as I have done, so God hath requited me. And they brought him to Jerusalem, and there he died.*

*8 Now the children of Judah had fought against Jerusalem, and had taken it, and smitten it with the edge of the sword, and set the city on fire.*

*9 And afterward the children of Judah went down to fight against the Canaanites, that dwelt in the mountain, and in the south, and in the valley.*

*10 And Judah went against the Canaanites that dwelt in Hebron: (now the name of Hebron before was Kirjatharba:) and they slew Sheshai, and Ahiman, and Talmai.*

*11 And from thence he went against the inhabitants of Debir: and the name of Debir before was Kirjathsepher:*

*12 And Caleb said, He that smiteth Kirjathsepher, and taketh it, to him will I give Achsah my daughter to wife.*

*13 And Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother, took it: and he gave him Achsah his daughter to wife.*

*14 And it came to pass, when she came to him, that she moved him to ask of her father a field: and she lighted from off her ass; and Caleb said unto her, What wilt thou?*

*15 And she said unto him, Give me a blessing: for thou hast given me a south land; give me also springs of water. And Caleb gave her the upper springs and the nether springs.*

*16 And the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law, went up out of the city of palm trees with the children of Judah into the wilderness of Judah, which lieth in the south of Arad; and they went and dwelt among the people.*

*17 And Judah went with Simeon his brother, and they slew the Canaanites that inhabited Zephath, and utterly destroyed it. And the name of the city was called Hormah.*

*18 Also Judah took Gaza with the coast thereof, and Askelon with the coast thereof, and Ekron with the coast thereof.*

*19 And the Lord was with Judah; and he drave out the inhabitants of the mountain; but could not drive out the inhabitants of the valley, because they had chariots of iron.*

*20 And they gave Hebron unto Caleb, as Moses said: and he expelled thence the three sons of Anak.*

*21 And the children of Benjamin did not drive out the Jebusites that inhabited Jerusalem; but the Jebusites dwell with the children of Benjamin in Jerusalem unto this day.*

*22 And the house of Joseph, they also went up against Bethel: and the Lord was with them.*

*23 And the house of Joseph sent to descry Bethel. (Now the name of the city before was Luz.)*

*24 And the spies saw a man come forth out of the city, and they said unto him, Shew us, we pray thee, the entrance into the city, and we will shew thee mercy.*

*25 And when he shewed them the entrance into the city, they smote the city with the edge of the sword; but they let go the man and all his family.*

*26 And the man went into the land of the Hittites, and built a city, and called the name thereof Luz: which is the name thereof unto this day.*

*27 Neither did Manasseh drive out the inhabitants of Bethshean and her towns, nor Taanach and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Dor and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Ibleam and her towns, nor the inhabitants of Megiddo and her towns: but the Canaanites would dwell in that land.*

*28 And it came to pass, when Israel was strong, that they put the Canaanites to tribute, and did not utterly drive them out.*

*29 Neither did Ephraim drive out the Canaanites that dwelt in Gezer; but the Canaanites dwelt in Gezer among them.*

*30 Neither did Zebulun drive out the inhabitants of Kitron, nor the inhabitants of Nahalol; but the Canaanites dwelt among them, and became tributaries.*

*31 Neither did Asher drive out the inhabitants of Accho, nor the inhabitants of Zidon, nor of Ahlab, nor of Achzib, nor of Helbah, nor of Aphik, nor of Rehob:*

*32 But the Asherites dwelt among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land: for they did not drive them out.*

*33 Neither did Naphtali drive out the inhabitants of Bethshemesh, nor the inhabitants of Bethanath; but he dwelt among the Canaanites, the inhabitants of the land: nevertheless the inhabitants of Bethshemesh and of Bethanath became tributaries unto them.*

*34 And the Amorites forced the children of Dan into the mountain: for they would not suffer them to come down to the valley:*

*35 But the Amorites would dwell in mount Heres in Aijalon, and in Shaalbim: yet the hand of the house of Joseph prevailed, so that they became tributaries.*

*36 And the coast of the Amorites was from the going up to Akrabbim, from the rock, and upward.*

**Judges 2**
*And an angel of the Lord came up from Gilgal to Bochim, and said, I made you to go up out of Egypt, and have brought you unto the land which I sware unto your fathers; and I said, I will never break my covenant with you.*

*2 And ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars: but ye have not obeyed my voice: why have ye done this?*

*3 Wherefore I also said, I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be as thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare unto you.*

*4 And it came to pass, when the angel of the Lord spake these words unto all the children of Israel, that the people lifted up their voice, and wept.*

*5 And they called the name of that place Bochim: and they sacrificed there unto the Lord.*

*6 And when Joshua had let the people go, the children of Israel went every man unto his inheritance to possess the land.*

*7 And the people served the Lord all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders that outlived Joshua, who had seen all the great works of the Lord, that he did for Israel.*

*8 And Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the Lord, died, being an hundred and ten years old.*

*9 And they buried him in the border of his inheritance in Timnathheres, in the mount of Ephraim, on the north side of the hill Gaash.*

*10 And also all that generation were gathered unto their fathers: and there arose another generation after them, which knew not the Lord, nor yet the works which he had done for Israel.*

*11 And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and served Baalim:*

*12 And they forsook the Lord God of their fathers, which brought them out of the land of Egypt, and followed other gods, of the gods of the people that were round about them, and bowed themselves unto them, and provoked the Lord to anger.*

*13 And they forsook the Lord, and served Baal and Ashtaroth.*

*14 And the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers that spoiled them, and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about, so that they could not any longer stand before their enemies.*

*15 Whithersoever they went out, the hand of the Lord was against them for evil, as the Lord had said, and as the Lord had sworn unto them: and they were greatly distressed.*

*16 Nevertheless the Lord raised up judges, which delivered them out of the hand of those that spoiled them.*

*17 And yet they would not hearken unto their judges, but they went a whoring after other gods, and bowed themselves unto them: they turned quickly out of the way which their fathers walked in, obeying the commandments of the Lord; but they did not so.*

*18 And when the Lord raised them up judges, then the Lord was with the judge, and delivered them out of the hand of their enemies all the days of the judge: for it repented the Lord because of their groanings by reason of them that oppressed them and vexed them.*

*19 And it came to pass, when the judge was dead, that they returned, and corrupted themselves more than their fathers, in following other gods to serve them, and to bow down unto them; they ceased not from their own doings, nor from their stubborn way.*

*20 And the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel; and he said, Because that this people hath transgressed my covenant which I commanded their fathers, and have not hearkened unto my voice;*

*21 I also will not henceforth drive out any from before them of the nations which Joshua left when he died:*

*22 That through them I may prove Israel, whether they will keep the way of the Lord to walk therein, as their fathers did keep it, or not.*

*23 Therefore the Lord left those nations, without driving them out hastily; neither delivered he them into the hand of Joshua.*

**Judges 1 & 2** sets the stage for the next era of Israel, following the death of Joshua. The various tribes failed to utterly destroy the Canaanites in the land God had given them to possess, and instead made tributaries of them. Valuing their gold more than God. Keeping these people among them, that they become thorns in their sides.

The corruption of the following generations, who turned from the deliverance of God and His covenant, was sown in the remnants of the heathen among them. They turned to worship Baal and Asteroth, 'the queen of heaven." They were beset and spoiled constantly by the remnants of the nations. The children of Israel were even taken as slaves.

And periodically, when the complaints of the Israelites were heard by God, he sent a judge. A deliverer to save them from their plight. And when the judge was dead, they returned to corruption and adultery with idols, following other gods.

The picture of Christ, the judge who delivers us from death and bondage, but who never dies, living forever the first fruits of the resurrection. Who will judge the quick and the dead at the judgment seat of Christ for saints, the great white throne for the unregenerate.

It is Christ Jesus, the angel of the Lord who appears before them to let them know that He would no longer drive the heathen from them, because they had not thrown down their altars and slain the people. The covenant He would never break was broken, *finding fault with them.*

Christians in the world, delivered by the most High Judge, Christ Jesus will see, their children and grandchildren fall away to the world, just as the tribes of Judah did. But the promise of His deliverance remains forever, that they may turn to Him and call upon His name and be saved.

We will see this patterned for us in **Judges**, again and again.

**Judges 1:28**
*And it came to pass, when Israel was strong, that they put the Canaanites to tribute, and did not utterly drive them out.*

**Judges 2:1-3**
*And an angel of the Lord came up from Gilgal to Bochim, and said, I made you to go up out of Egypt, and have brought you unto the land which I sware unto your fathers; and I said, I will never break my covenant with you. And ye shall make no league with the inhabitants of this land; ye shall throw down their altars: but ye have not obeyed my voice: why have ye done this? Wherefore I also said, I will not drive them out from before you; but they shall be as thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare unto you.*

**Judges 2:11-14**
*And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and served Baalim: And they forsook the Lord God of their fathers, which brought them out of the land of Egypt, and followed other gods, of the gods of the people that were round about them, and bowed themselves unto them, and provoked the Lord to anger. And the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel, and he delivered them into the hands of spoilers that spoiled them, and he sold them into the hands of their enemies round about, so that they could not any longer stand before their enemies.*

**Judges 2:20-23**
*And the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel; and he said, Because that this people hath transgressed my covenant which I commanded their fathers, and have not hearkened unto my voice; I also will not henceforth drive out any from before them of the nations which Joshua left when he died: That through them I may prove Israel, whether they will keep the way of the Lord to walk therein, as their fathers did keep it, or not. Therefore the Lord left those nations, without driving them out hastily; neither delivered he them into the hand of Joshua.*

**Judges 3:1-4**
*Now these are the nations which the Lord left, to prove Israel by them, even as many of Israel as had not known all the wars of Canaan; Only that the generations of the children of Israel might know, to teach them war, at the least such as before knew nothing thereof; Namely, five lords of the Philistines, and all the Canaanites, and the Sidonians, and the Hivites that dwelt in mount Lebanon, from mount Baalhermon unto the entering in of Hamath. And they were to prove Israel by them, to know whether they would hearken unto the commandments of the Lord, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.*

Just to recap the theme going into the **Book of Judges**; God having delivered the people into the promised land commanded them to utterly destroy the inhabitants and to smash down their altars to the false gods they worshipped. The Lord had been with them in every battle (save one, thanks to the abomination of Achan). He had driven out the people that Joshua and his armies went against. He delivered 33 Kings into their hands. The Lord God rained hail the size of boulders, drove men out with hornets, felled the walls of cities with the shout and trumpets of the Israelites.

But yet they did not fully eradicate the Canaanites and others in the land. They resorted to allowing them to stay in tribute. Valuing their gold more than the commandments of God.

They had the knowledge of the will of the sovereign God, and *chose*, of their own will, to ignore His word, to do as they saw was right in their own eyes. Despite all their valiant deeds and the miracles they witnessed while obeying Him, they slacked off in their duty to do that which was comfortable. Easy. To leave the work unfinished.

By their choice. By free will.

And God responded by removing the hedge of protection around them. By allowing them to feel the consequences of their actions. By using these nations as a thorn in the side of Israel, to prove her that they may learn the ways of war, rather than peace. To be a snare with their false gods, so that the glory of God could be known. That in their tribulation they would call out to the Lord for salvation, and He would place His Spirit on a judge He would raise up to deliver them.

The Bible is the record of God's will for man, in Christ Jesus. And it demonstrates that He gave His word as a testimony, that man should believe Him. The Godhead being three persons, that the witness be true, just as the law requires. Jesus appeared resurrected to witnesses that others believed their report. The Spirit indwells believers, that it testify to them they have eternal life, that they may **know**. The Bible exists, inspired and preserved, that we may hear the word and have faith that it is true, and obey His commandments beginning with the gospel of Christ.

It is always a choice. And God uses our choices to His purpose, even when we are disobedient. Even when some don't believe the report. Even when people fall away from the truth.

Calvinism demands that a sovereign God removes that choice, the need for His word as testimony, the Spirit to believe, and makes all of man's shortcomings God's responsibility. It denies the power of God to see His will done **despite** our failings. To use our sins as a means of shaping the clay as a Potter.

The covenants become worthless, because why make promises and give blessings for man's obedience when the obedience is given to them?

The Israelites failed to harken to the commandments of God, and lost those blessings and protections. Just as the covenant with Moses in the wilderness established as terms; I will be your God, and ye shall be My people. But if they took up the gods and abominations of those in the land, it would be a curse, and they would be troubled until they turned back to the Lord.

The covenant was glorious, but the fault was with them.

None of this makes sense in a Calvinistic world view. There is no lesson to learn from it. If they were predestinated to disobey, then the punishment they received wouldn't be to prove them and provoke them to repentance. God's decision to let them suffer the consequences to teach them their need for salvation in Him wouldn't make any sense. There's no need for the law to be a schoolmaster if faith and obedience is handed down by the good will of a sovereign Lord, on whomever He will.

And it limits God, showing He needs total control of man's actions in order to have the outcome He desires, rather than the glory and power of His will being done despite man's disobedience.

And it makes Christ's obedience to the Father's will unto death meaningless, for if man's obedience is forced upon them, why would the Son saying "not my will, but the Father's" mean anything at all to us? How would that perfect obedience save us? How is it an inspiration to strive for that perfection?

The gospel of the Calvinist is a hopeless thing, and their false god is weak and capricious.

**2 Timothy 2:16-19**
*But shun profane and vain babblings: for they will increase unto more ungodliness. And their word will eat as doth a canker: of whom is Hymenaeus and Philetus; Who concerning the truth have erred, saying that the resurrection is past already; and overthrow the faith of some. Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.*

**Acts 1:6-11**
*When they therefore were come together, they asked of him, saying, Lord, wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel? And he said unto them, It is not for you to know the times or the seasons, which the Father hath put in his own power. But ye shall receive power, after that the Holy Ghost is come upon you: and ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth. **2 Peter 3:1-4;8**
*This second epistle, beloved, I now write unto you; in both which I stir up your pure minds by way of remembrance: That ye may be mindful of the words which were spoken before by the holy prophets, and of the commandment of us the apostles of the Lord and Saviour: Knowing this first, that there shall come in the last days scoffers, walking after their own lusts, And saying, Where is the promise of his coming? for since the fathers fell asleep, all things continue as they were from the beginning of the creation...But, beloved, be not ignorant of this one thing, that one day is with the Lord as a thousand years, and a thousand years as one day.*

**Judges 3**
*Now these are the nations which the Lord left, to prove Israel by them, even as many of Israel as had not known all the wars of Canaan;*

*2 Only that the generations of the children of Israel might know, to teach them war, at the least such as before knew nothing thereof;*

*3 Namely, five lords of the Philistines, and all the Canaanites, and the Sidonians, and the Hivites that dwelt in mount Lebanon, from mount Baalhermon unto the entering in of Hamath.*

*4 And they were to prove Israel by them, to know whether they would hearken unto the commandments of the Lord, which he commanded their fathers by the hand of Moses.*

*5 And the children of Israel dwelt among the Canaanites, Hittites, and Amorites, and Perizzites, and Hivites, and Jebusites:*

*6 And they took their daughters to be their wives, and gave their daughters to their sons, and served their gods.*

*7 And the children of Israel did evil in the sight of the Lord, and forgat the Lord their God, and served Baalim and the groves.*

*8 Therefore the anger of the Lord was hot against Israel, and he sold them into the hand of Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia: and the children of Israel served Chushanrishathaim eight years.*

*9 And when the children of Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord raised up a deliverer to the children of Israel, who delivered them, even Othniel the son of Kenaz, Caleb's younger brother.*

*10 And the Spirit of the Lord came upon him, and he judged Israel, and went out to war: and the Lord delivered Chushanrishathaim king of Mesopotamia into his hand; and his hand prevailed against Chushanrishathaim.*

*11 And the land had rest forty years. And Othniel the son of Kenaz died.*

*12 And the children of Israel did evil again in the sight of the Lord: and the Lord strengthened Eglon the king of Moab against Israel, because they had done evil in the sight of the Lord.*

*13 And he gathered unto him the children of Ammon and Amalek, and went and smote Israel, and possessed the city of palm trees.*

*14 So the children of Israel served Eglon the king of Moab eighteen years.*

*15 But when the children of Israel cried unto the Lord, the Lord raised them up a deliverer, Ehud the son of Gera, a Benjamite, a man lefthanded: and by him the children of Israel sent a present unto Eglon the king of Moab.*

*16 But Ehud made him a dagger which had two edges, of a cubit length; and he did gird it under his raiment upon his right thigh.*

*17 And he brought the present unto Eglon king of Moab: and Eglon was a very fat man.*

*18 And when he had made an end to offer the present, he sent away the people that bare the present.*

*19 But he himself turned again from the quarries that were by Gilgal, and said, I have a secret errand unto thee, O king: who said, Keep silence. And all that stood by him went out from him.*

*20 And Ehud came unto him; and he was sitting in a summer parlour, which he had for himself alone. And Ehud said, I have a message from God unto thee. And he arose out of his seat.*

*21 And Ehud put forth his left hand, and took the dagger from his right thigh, and thrust it into his belly:*

*22 And the haft also went in after the blade; and the fat closed upon the blade, so that he could not draw the dagger out of his belly; and the dirt came out.*

*23 Then Ehud went forth through the porch, and shut the doors of the parlour upon him, and locked them.*

*24 When he was gone out, his servants came; and when they saw that, behold, the doors of the parlour were locked, they said, Surely he covereth his feet in his summer chamber.*

*25 And they tarried till they were ashamed: and, behold, he opened not the doors of the parlour; therefore they took a key, and opened them: and, behold, their lord was fallen down dead on the earth.*

*26 And Ehud escaped while they tarried, and passed beyond the quarries, and escaped unto Seirath.*

*27 And it came to pass, when he was come, that he blew a trumpet in the mountain of Ephraim, and the children of Israel went down with him from the mount, and he before them.*

*28 And he said unto them, Follow after me: for the Lord hath delivered your enemies the Moabites into your hand. And they went down after him, and took the fords of Jordan toward Moab, and suffered not a man to pass over.*

*29 And they slew of Moab at that time about ten thousand men, all lusty, and all men of valour; and there escaped not a man.*

*30 So Moab was subdued that day under the hand of Israel. And the land had rest fourscore years.*

*31 And after him was Shamgar the son of Anath, which slew of the Philistines six hundred men with an ox goad: and he also delivered Israel.*

The pattern of falling away, turning to God for deliverance, and God sending a judge to free the children of Israel begins.

We see that God determines that the heathen in the land that they had failed to utterly remove will serve as a means to test the people, to keep them ready for war, to humble them, to tempt them to marry their outlandish woman and worship their false gods.

And when they suffered the fruit of their adultery, and came to see their need for God's salvation, repented towards Him, and called upon His name, He would send a deliverer.

In the same way, tribulation and sin in the world serve to test man, and as a schoolmaster, bring people to be humbled before God and seek His help. To call upon the name of Christ, the judge of all, to deliver us.

The Jews, who say they are but are not and do lie, exist in this world for the same reason these Canaanites do. The same with every evil organization of men.

They are here to keep us spiritually equipped for war. To tempt us into sin and worship of false gods. To test us and try us. To bring us to Him.

You can almost hear an ancient Israelite saying "of God real, why bad things happen? Why Chushanrishathaim attack us?"

Here in Judges we see exactly why. And it is to glory God.

Now in the narrative we see the early history of the Israelites in the promised land. The 5 lords of the Philistines, Sidonians, Hivites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Moabites, Jebusites, and Canaanites in general, are both bordering and among the land inherited by each tribe.

The king of Mesopotamia, Chushanrishathaim comes against them and leads them as captives 8 years, and Caleb's nephew Othneil has the Spirit of the Lord come up on him, and he as judge delivers the Mesopotamian into his hands. And for 40 years they knew peace. And Othneil dies.

The 40 year pattern is a generational cycle used by God throughout history. The wandering in the wilderness. The cycle of judges and kings. The time between Pentecost and the ascension of Jesus to the destruction of the temple and Jerusalem in 70AD...God provides a span of these generations to allow man to get right, as He judges nations.

Next we see Moab come up against Israel as the agent of God's wrath for Israel for falling away again. The children of Ammon and Amalek, who take possession of Jericho, the city of palm trees. And for 18 years the children of Israel serve under Eglon.

And when Israel cried unto the Lord for deliverance, Ehud, a Benjamite was raised up by the Lord as judge. And Ehud, the left-handed judge slays Eglon in God's name, in one of the most gruesome deaths of the Bible.

Judges has some of the best narratives ever, better than those Netflix and HBO could ever imagine.

And after the destruction of the Moabites under Ehud, the land knows rest for 80 years.

Then we learn of Shamgar son of Anath, who slew 600 Philistines with an ox goad, an unimaginable feat, yet relegated to a single verse. (We will see another mention of Shamgar in a few chapters, in the song of Deborah)

But we see the pattern. The harder the times, the more likely the people turn to the Lord. The better the times, the quicker they fall away.

In our Christian life, we may see similar patterns. There's a tendency towards leaning on God, turning to prayer more often, reading the Bible more, increasing church attendance, maybe even fasting...but when the deliverance comes, many begin to shirk those things. And rather than walk in the Spirit, backslide towards walking in the flesh.

God uses tribulation to prove us. That we may learn to trust Him more, to increase our faith. To learn mercy and judgement. To increase patience.

We see it throughout the Epistles.

**Romans 5:1-5**
*Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ: By whom also we have access by faith into this grace wherein we stand, and rejoice in hope of the glory of God. And not only so, but we glory in tribulations also: knowing that tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed; because the love of God is shed abroad in our hearts by the Holy Ghost which is given unto us.*

It's the same pattern, spiritual rather than physical, but similar. A picture of our Christian life.

**Judges 4**
*And the children of Israel again did evil in the sight of the Lord, when Ehud was dead.*

*2 And the Lord sold them into the hand of Jabin king of Canaan, that reigned in Hazor; the captain of whose host was Sisera, which dwelt in Harosheth of the Gentiles.*

*3 And the children of Israel cried unto the Lord: for he had nine hundred chariots of iron; and twenty years he mightily oppressed the children of Israel.*

*4 And Deborah, a prophetess, the wife of Lapidoth, she judged Israel at that time.*

*5 And she dwelt under the palm tree of Deborah between Ramah and Bethel in mount Ephraim: and the children of Israel came up to her for judgment.*

*6 And she sent and called Barak the son of Abinoam out of Kedeshnaphtali, and said unto him, Hath not the Lord God of Israel commanded, saying, Go and draw toward mount Tabor, and take with thee ten thousand men of the children of Naphtali and of the children of Zebulun?*

*7 And I will draw unto thee to the river Kishon Sisera, the captain of Jabin's army, with his chariots and his multitude; and I will deliver him into thine hand.*

*8 And Barak said unto her, If thou wilt go with me, then I will go: but if thou wilt not go with me, then I will not go.*

*9 And she said, I will surely go with thee: notwithstanding the journey that thou takest shall not be for thine honour; for the Lord shall sell Sisera into the hand of a woman. And Deborah arose, and went with Barak to Kedesh.*

*10 And Barak called Zebulun and Naphtali to Kedesh; and he went up with ten thousand men at his feet: and Deborah went up with him.*

*11 Now Heber the Kenite, which was of the children of Hobab the father in law of Moses, had severed himself from the Kenites, and pitched his tent unto the plain of Zaanaim, which is by Kedesh.*

*12 And they shewed Sisera that Barak the son of Abinoam was gone up to mount Tabor.*

*13 And Sisera gathered together all his chariots, even nine hundred chariots of iron, and all the people that were with him, from Harosheth of the Gentiles unto the river of Kishon.*

*14 And Deborah said unto Barak, Up; for this is the day in which the Lord hath delivered Sisera into thine hand: is not the Lord gone out before thee? So Barak went down from mount Tabor, and ten thousand men after him.*

*15 And the Lord discomfited Sisera, and all his chariots, and all his host, with the edge of the sword before Barak; so that Sisera lighted down off his chariot, and fled away on his feet.*

*16 But Barak pursued after the chariots, and after the host, unto Harosheth of the Gentiles: and all the host of Sisera fell upon the edge of the sword; and there was not a man left.*

*17 Howbeit Sisera fled away on his feet to the tent of Jael the wife of Heber the Kenite: for there was peace between Jabin the king of Hazor and the house of Heber the Kenite.*

*I am pursuing after Zebah and Zalmunna, kings of Midian. And the princes of Succoth said, Are the hands of Zebah and Zalmunna now in thine hand, that we should give bread unto thine army?*

The men of the next community, Penuel respond the same way.

Gideon vows that when he returns, he will take thorns as scourges against the men of Succoth and tear down the tower of Penuel. A vow he fulfilled after he and his men capture the fleeing princes, Zebah and Zalmunna, whipping and killing the men and razing the tower.

Gideon tells his captives, Zebah and Zalmunna, that had they spared lives of those at Tabor, an apparent raid they'd conducted in Israel, he would have spared their lives.

Gideon asks his young son to take the heads of the princes, but by his youth he can't do it. Gideon takes them instead, after Zebah and Zalmunna mock him.

So the armies were defeated and the children of Israel took the spoil and returned back across the Jordan, hailing Gideon for delivering them out of the hands of the Midianites.

They call for Gideon to be made king and his son and future sons to rule over them. But Gideon meekly declined, giving glory to God.

However, he does ask for tribute. The gold earrings of the men slain, which when taken together was a substantial weight of gold. And while judging Israel the rest of his days, back in Ophrah of Manasseh, he takes the gold of his spoil and makes himself an ephod. A golden vestment of the office of the high priest.

This is the snare of Gideon. This causes the children of Israel to go a whoring.

Some interpretations of this make the ephod an idol that is worshipped, but it seems unlikely that Jerubbaal, aka Gideon, a smasher of idols, "the accused of Baal," would set up an idol and there's no indication that they worshipped the ephod itself.

It is more likely in my opinion to mean that Gideon, despite his declining to be a king, allowed his popularity and fame to make him seek to usurp the place God chose, Shiloh, and the office of the high priest to whom the Ephod crafted by Moses belonged. And rather than go to Shiloh for spiritual matters, many in Israel came down to Ophrah and Gideon.

The number of wives and sons he produced showed that he did take advantage of his glory, despite deferring the glory of the victory to God. The spoils he took as tribute became a snare, and caused the Israelites to go whoring, away from the commandment of the Lord.

So we see, even Gideon, full of fear. Requiring signs. Witnessing the miracle of their defeat of a troop of over a hundred and fifty thousand with 300 men, let his success go to his head. Leading him to sin.

This is a trap some very successful Christians fall in to. Who have been used mightily for God, and done great works for Him. For all their humility and understanding that it was not of them, pride eats away at their character. God's success begins to seem to them to be a partnership. And their *idea* of what God wants take the place of what God actually wills for them.

We can apply this to great modern preachers of the word, who have won thousands of souls to Christ, and then, building an empire from the success, sow the seeds their own downfall.

And the people who they helped forget these men, after they've died. And their children turn to wickedness. Worshiping Baal as the Israelites do. The children of these great soldiers for God not turning out to be godly men, but wicked, like Gideon's son, Abimelech.

Here in **Judges 9** we are given the story of Abimelech, one of the 70 sons of Gideon, also known as Jerubbaal, and his brief, violent and wicked time as king over Shechem.

Shechem is a city north of Jerusalem and south of Samaria, in the center of Canaan, on the west Bank of the Jordan. It is where Abraham built an altar to God upon the covenant he received, and where Jacob pitched his tents. It is where his sons, Levi and Simeon killed all the men, after their sister Dinah was raped.

Shechem is where Joshua assembled the children of Israel and asked them to choose this day whom they would serve, the gods of Babylon , beyond the Euphrates; Baal and Asteroth who were the gods of the Canaanites or the living God Who had led them from Egypt and given them the promised land. It became a Levitical city in Ephraim, a city of refuge.

Gideon had taken a concubine from among the people of Shechem, from among the ruling families, and her son was Abimelech.

And so, after the death of Gideon, with the people of Israel forgetting the Lord God and worshiping Baal-Berith, they had built a temple to the false "god of the covenant" there, and it is in Shechem Abimelech goes to seek power.

Not content to share the diminishing power of being a son of Gideon with his 70 brothers, Abimelech curries favor with his mother's kin in Shechem, and in exchange for a piece of silver from the temple of Berith, one per brother, gathers a gang of base fellows, vain and light, to set about slaying them.

They succeeded in murdering them all up on a rock, save one, Jotham. Jotham curses Abimelech and the men of the city for their treachery, saying by allegory that Israel had great men before it that refused to be king, represented by the olive, the fig and the vine, and yet they chose the worst, a briar. The bramble. And that by doing so Abimelech would destroy them by fire.

Jotham then flees, hiding in Beer.

And so for 3 years, the cruel king rules in Shechem, and the men of the city grow disillusioned by their choice because *God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem*. Their trust was diminished, and they sought to deal with their king treacherously. They hired a band of men to lay in wait for him in the mountains, men who robbed all who passed by, and Abimelech was made aware of their plans.

The bandits failing them, the men turned to one of their own, Gaal son of Ebed. Gaal, his men and the men of the city get drunk, and Gaal curses Abimelech, Zebul his chief officer and ruler of the city, and promises to rule in place of the king after overthrowing the son of Jerubbaal.

Zebul hears of it and informs Abimelech, and they plot to surround the city and take it to put down the rebellion.

When Gaal sees the companies of men surrounding the city, Zebul at first taunts him, questioning his senses, saying he is afraid of shadows. But then tells Gaal that here is his chance, go out and fight Abimelech the same who he had cursed. Abimelech defeats the men, and they flee into the city but Zebul throws the rebels out. Abimelech's men slay them and turn towards the city and take it. Slaughtering the men and burning down the tower and the temple and salting the earth, Jotham's curse fufiled.

Not satisfied with the destruction of Shechem, Abimelech moves on the city of Thebez, which too has a strong tower, a keep in the center of the city. The last refuge for siege in the walled cities. And like the tower of Shechem, Gideon's son begins to light fire to the door, to burn the tower down with the people inside.

And a woman throws down a piece of millstone, that grinds the wheat to flour, and it hit Abimelech in the head, breaking his skull. And the wicked wannabe king calls his armourbearer and begs him to run him through with a sword, so no one could say he was killed by a woman. Reminiscent of the death of Sisera by the hand of Jael.

*And when the men of Israel saw that Abimelech was dead, they departed every man unto his place.*

The brief civil war was over.

*Thus God rendered the wickedness of Abimelech, which he did unto his father, in slaying his seventy brethren: And all the evil of the men of Shechem did God render upon their heads: and upon them came the curse of Jotham the son of Jerubbaal.*
The book of Judges is better than any Hollywood blockbuster or Netflix series. The Sopranos has nothing on Jerubbaal, Abimelech and the rest of these men. I love God's word.

Abimelech serves as a picture of a type found throughout scripture, and the pattern we see even today. Mighty man of the Lord does great works and has a son that's prodigal or worse, wicked. Some misguided, some reprobate.

The children of Jacob, to varying degrees. The sons of Aaron. Gideon and Abimelech. David and Absolom.

Ultimately, it is a picture of God and fallen man. The Good King and his wayward or wicked son. The pastor and the pastor's son.

It seems that great men of God, who do good and mighty works for the Lord, often produce a child or two who openly rebel against them. Who become prodigal. And at times the father is unable to handle the truth and enables their offspring's wickedness. And others who do the right thing, choosing God over their own, and casting them out to be destroyed by their own wickedness.

We as parents have an obligation, a Godly duty, to be a picture of God's unconditional love and grace, forgiving our children's sins without enabling them. Chastening them when needed, but like the father of the Prodigal, rushing to meet them when they come home. To not be hypocrites. To live the example that we hold them to.

To be strong enough to cast out the reprobate. To bring an unruly son to the gates to be stoned.

Our behavior as parents is how children learn about God. It is an awesome responsibility, and one even the most separated fathers can fail at. Even as we, knowing God, fall away to sin, children will ultimately choose their way.

And so you have examples of men like Jack Hyles, who built an ephod of the spoils given him by God. A Bible college. A high school. Bus ministries and other things he took pride in, put his name on, along with the fame and respect that came with it.

And he had a son, David, who was wicked as Hell. An Abimelech.

But these things do not detract from the great works of the Lord, who uses men to do His will. They just show the weakness of the vessel. Jack Hyles was a mighty preacher, won hundreds of not thousands to the Lord. But the snare of pride led to the downfall of what he built.

It's tragic and sad. But it does not undo the mighty works done by God, just as Abimelech didn't change the deliverance of Israel under his father.

If you know any pastors who may be struggling with an unruly son or daughter, pray for them. Use discernment. Keep the works of God separate from the failures of men. God will repay.

We are here in **Judges 11**, and the story of Jephthah the Gileadite, son of a whore and the eponymous patriarch of Gilead. We are told he was a mighty man of valor, who by the jealousy and resentment of his half-brothers, was cast out of the community. He went to the wasteland, the land of Tob, and there he formed a gang of vain men, outlaws.

But when the children of Ammon came and made war against them, the elders of Gilead called for him to return and to be captain of their troops. Jephthah agrees so long as they pledge to make him their ruler, and they vow to God they will if he delivers them from the Ammonites.

Now, we know Jephthah is a man of faith, who *uttered all his words before the Lord*, taking on the responsibility of leadership in His name. He also is given honorable mention in the 'Hall of Faith' in **Hebrews 11:32-34**;

*And what shall I more say? for the time would fail me to tell of Gedeon, and of Barak, and of Samson, and of Jephthae; of David also, and Samuel, and of the prophets: Who through faith subdued kingdoms, wrought righteousness, obtained promises, stopped the mouths of lions. Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.*

And so, after his own pledge and profession of his faith, he rode out with men of Gilead and confronted the king of Ammon. Jephthah asks why they are attacking Israel, and the king responds that it is retribution for the taking of their land 300 years prior, as the children of Israel approached the promised land.

Jephthah, showing knowledge of their history, reminds them that the Ammonites brought it up on themselves, attacking the Israelites as they sought to pass between their coasts. That in the centuries since, the Ammonite kings accepted their loss of land. He says that since the Lord God had given the children of Israel the land by driving out the previous inhabitants, it was theirs. And he taunts their false god Chemosh, saying wouldn't they accept any land as their possession of it drove out the people?

And after this history lesson, Jephthah calls on the Lord the Judge to judge between them. And the Spirit of the Lord comes down, He delivers the Ammonites into the hands of Israel.

The Spirit of the Lord was upon him. He was definitely a man of faith. But yet, as Barak needed Deborah with him, and Gideon needed the dew upon the flax, Jephthah vowed a vow unto the Lord to assure his victory over the children of Ammon. That he would sacrifice whatsoever crossed his doorway when he returned from battle victorious, if the Lord delivered the enemy into his hands.

Returning victorious, he came to Mizpeh and his house, and there was his only child, his young daughter come to meet him. He rent his clothes and cried; *Alas, my daughter!*

His daughter tells him he must honor his vow to the Lord. Especially now that He had delivered victory and given him his enemies in vengeance.

She only asks to have 2 months to travel the mountains lamenting her death in virginity, which he grants. Sacrificing her as he vowed to do. Her story creating a custom in Israel among her daughters, that 4 days a year they lamented her plight.

As Jesus says, *Swear not at all; neither by heaven; for it is God's throne: Nor by the earth; for it is his footstool: neither by Jerusalem; for it is the city of the great King. Neither shalt thou swear by thy head, because thou canst not make one hair white or black.*

God does not need our vows, our promises to do good or to perform works in order to deliver us. He simply asks we trust in Him and let our *yea mean yea.*

Jephthah would have won victory over the children of Ammon by the power of the Lord. He did not need to add his own works as part of God's plan. But God holds us to vows;

**Ecclesiastes 5:4**
*When thou vowest a vow unto God, defer not to pay it; for he hath no pleasure in fools: pay that which thou hast vowed.*

So it should not be done in an idle fashion. But if possible, a vow to God in exchange for His favor should not be done at all. Godly living and honest character do not require such a thing. It is by God mighty hand that we are delivered. Not of works of ourselves.

Jephthah paid a price he needn't have, because he placed a portion of his faith in his own hands.

This shows that even just a few hundred years since Moses and the settling of the land by Israel, that distinct dialects and regional accents had occurred. God sets boundaries and habitations, dividing nations by blood and language, shifting over time as He judges them.

Samson begins the story by going into the cities of the Philistines, down from Dan to Timnath, and a Philistine girl there catches his eye. He returns to his parents and tells them to get her for him to wife.

Naturally, his parents are upset at this, that he would want an outlandish woman, unclean, to wed. They ask why not a woman from their tribe or from Israel, a fellow believer, a daughter of the circumcision. He insists and they relent, not knowing that this was of the Lord. That it was an opportunity for Samson to get in with the Philistines who were oppressing Israel.

As he makes his way back to Timnath, he encounters a young lion and tears it apart with his bare hands, by the power of the Spirit of the Lord. It is a supernatural act of strength, as an unarmed man rends a lion apart as a normal man could a baby goat. Samson, having touched an unclean thing, tells not his father or mother.

Samson talks with the woman, and she pleases him. Time passes, and on his way back to take her as a wife, he notices the carcass of the lion and that a bee hive has set up in it, producing honey. He reaches into this dead, unclean carcass and takes of the honey with his bare hands, and eats it and gives it to his parents to eat, without telling them where it came from.

The wedding is arranged and Samson makes a feast lasting 7 days, and having no groomsmen among the people, 30 Philistine men are made his companions. Samson offers them a bet in the form of a riddle, the stakes, 30 sheets and 30 sets of clothes.

The men agree, and Samson says *Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness*, referring to the lion and the honey. An impossible riddle that even his parents would be unable to solve.

And after 3 days of fruitless guessing, the 30nmen threaten the would-be bride and her family to pry the answer from Samson. She begs and pleads for the next several days and on the final day of the feast, Samson tells her the answer. His physical strength is mighty, but his weakness, as we will see throughout his story, is women.

The 30 companions tell Samson the answer, and he knows they cheated. *If ye had not plowed with my heifer, ye had not found out my riddle.*

And the Spirit of the Lord comes upon him, and he travels to a neighboring city and slays 30 Philistines in Ashkelon, taking from their unclean dead bodies the spoils of 30 sheets and sets of raiment, to pay of his bet.

Samson then returns to his father unmarried, and the girl is given to one of the 30 Philistine men who served as his companions.

It is always interesting to me when I read the story of Samson, how often he violated the vow of separation he was meant to live by. But his temper and his love of women would be his undoing.

In the final chapter of **Judges**, we see how fallen the children of Israel have come, doing only what is right in their own eyes.

We have seen them fail to drive the Canaanites out of the land, worshiping their idols, being led by women, their holiest man under a lifetime vow, whoring and eating unclean things. Setting up their own churches and establishing their own priesthood with idols and images. Wicked stuff.

And then, Benjamin wiped out down to 600 men, because they harbored and protected reprobate sodomites in the land, commiting abominations. Raping a woman to death because the man they sought was refused them.

And that man, horrifyingly sending parts of her corpse to the tribes, seeking vengeance. And those tribes in turn being smitten by the sword, until they finally got right enough with God to win their over their own brethren, Benjamin.

**Judges** is a wicked period in the history of Israel, and yet it is also a common thing in all nations that do not seek after the Lord or have Him as King over them. Even with the perfect law, a comprehensive religion and the underlying promise of salvation by faith in Him, calling upon His name, Israel are lost without a strong human leader.

While there were undoubtedly saved believers in Israel, and they were meant to be a light to all nations, their own brethren fell away to apostasy and sin.

Here in **Judges 21**, we see even when trying to do the right thing, men left to their own heart still do that which is wicked.

The men who went up to war from all of Israel, repented of their slaughter of Benjamin. Note, God had ultimately approved of it, giving them victory and delivering Benjamin to them.

But they then second guess themselves. They change their mind and lament that they've put out one of the tribes, condemning it to death, because even with the remnant of 600 men, hiding out in the rock Rimmon, they had no wives or children. And the men of Israel who had gathered in the assembly at Mizpeh had sworns an oath to God that none would give their daughters to Benjamin to wife.

Faxed with this quandary of their own making, they seek out a solution that would be right in their own eyes.

Of course, God teaches us about vows. That we shouldn't vow at all. But if we do, follow through.

Realizing that of all the assembly, the men of Jabeshgilead failed to come down to Mizpeh. They had foresaken the assembly, and thus had not made the vow about wives for Benjamin. And the men at Mizpeh had additionally vowed to slay any who forsook the assembly.

And so the gathered army turned on Jabeshgilead, killing all the men and women who had lain with men, kidnapping 400 virgins, and offering them to the remnant of Benjamin. And understanding they were 200 short, strike a deal with the Benjamites that they would allow them to go to a feast at Shiloh and take 200 daughters who they could capture while they danced in the fields. Their fathers and brethren would not be held to the vow, for they weren't given but taken by force.

A wicked solution to a wicked situation.

None of this was from God. And when we Seek to do that which is right in our own eyes, error compounds error. Sin begets worse sin.

Had everyone kept to the law, obeying the commandments of God, heeding His ways, it would have been well with them. Israel would have been a light to the world, leading the nations to God.

Instead they fell short. They put themselves in terrible positions, and constantly needed a deliverer to save them when doing what seemed right in their own eyes failed them.

The book of Judges is a difficult one, detailing the history between the settling of Israel under Joshua, and before the era of kings that begins with Saul. There are great heroes in the book, like Gideon and Sampson, but the key lesson throughout is that not everyone in the Bible behaves righteously. Many are wicked and sinful. The key to understanding is found in the often-repeated verse; *In those days there was no king in Israel: every man did that which was right in his own eyes.*

That's the larger context. That even when the people turn to the Lord and do the right thing, it isn't always for the right reasons and many times they just do what they think is right in their own eyes.

All this to say the story told in Judges 19-21, of the sodomites protected within the tribe of Benjamin, and God's command to smite the tribe, He giving the others of Israel victory over them for their condoning and protecting these wicked sons of Belial, is very illustrative of the times we live in today, where people do what is right in their own eyes. Regardless of anything else; people were rightfully shocked and disgusted by the actions of the sodomites, and the willingness of Benjamin to fight to the death to protect those abominations. The fracture this war against a fellow tribe caused many divisions as we see. Much death. But the sodomites and most of their protectors were removed from the land.

Regardless of anything else, even with the common sin and day to day failure of most to walk with the Lord or to do what is right in His sight, the presence of sons of Belial in the land is seen as a greater threat and so great an offense to God, that the people mounted an army and went to war.
